description: "Passionate space science enthusiast and technologist specializing in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). Eager to bridge the gap between advanced data systems and aerospace applications, turning complex multi-mission data into actionable tools for space exploration and human safety.Dedicated to building intelligent, data-driven systems that make human spaceflight safer, smarter, and more efficient."
summary:
What we developed:
 Astronav is an interactive web map of Jezero Crater, Mars, that brings elevation, relief shading and a slope and walkability layer into one view. It also includes science stops, example routes, a route planner between any two places, a spacewalk-fit calculator, and weather conditions measured by NASA’s Perseverance rover.

How it addresses the challenge:
 It combines data from multiple NASA missions into one layered view for planning a Marswalk. Terrain from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter images becomes a slope map, and Perseverance weather readings add surface conditions. Astronav then compares the straight-line route with a safer path found by searching for the gentlest ground. For the base-to-delta trip, the steepest slope drops from 26.1° to 5.1°.

Why it is important:
 Astronauts will need to judge terrain, distance and time before stepping outside. Astronav makes that planning visible and easy to understand, and it states its limits clearly.Astronav is a learning and planning aid for exploring Marswalk routes.
details:
What does AstroNav do and How does it work?

Astronav is an interactive map of Jezero Crater, Mars. Users can drag and zoom the map, switch layers on and off (relief shading, elevation colour, and a slope and walkability layer), and select markers for the base, science stops and valleys. It also has a route planner between any two places, a guided tour, a “check a path” tool that measures a path you click, and a spacewalk-fit calculator.

Under the hood, slope is calculated from a 20 m terrain model and coloured easy (under 10°), harder (10° to 20°) or very steep (over 20°). For each route, Astronav compares the straight line with a safe path found by searching 40 m cells for the gentlest ground, avoiding cells steeper than 20°. It reports distance, steepest slope and total climbing for both, and checks whether the round trip fits inside a spacewalk at the chosen walking speed and length.

Benefits of AstroNav :

It shows that the straight line is not always the safest line. For the base-to-delta trip, the steepest slope drops from 26.1° (straight line) to 5.1° (safe path).

It puts terrain, routes, timing and measured weather in one place instead of across separate datasets.

It works in a browser on phone and desktop, with no install.

It states its assumptions and limits openly, so users know how far to trust it.

It's Intended impact :

To make Marswalk planning easier to see and understand for students, space enthusiasts and early-stage planners, and to serve as a base that others can extend with more data (radiation, boulder hazards, more routes). It is a learning and planning aid, not mission-control software.

Tools , Languages , Software used :

Languages : HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python.

Web : SVG (route overlays), PNG image layers (relief shading, elevation colour, slope and walkability).

Data Processing : Python scripts for slope calculation and safe-route search, using the USGS Mars 2020 CTX DEM (20 m).

Hosting and Verion Control : GitHub, GitHub Pages.

Presentation : Canva (demo slides)

Software : Visual Studio Code, Google Sheets (team research).

AI Tools: GitHub Copilot (code suggestions and updates to the website code), Claude (guidance, code review, drafting text).

Creativity :

Astronav turns raw Mars terrain data into an interactive tool people can explore. Users compare the straight-line route with a safe path found by searching for the gentlest ground. On the base-to-delta trip, the steepest slope drops from 26.1° to 5.1°.

A spacewalk-fit calculator with adjustable walking speed and spacewalk length shows whether a trip fits in one spacewalk. A guided tour, a route planner and a "check a path" tool make the map easy to explore.


Factors we considered :

Slope limits: We used 10° as "easy" (our planning assumption) and 20° as "very steep," following NASA's lunar suit requirement. That standard is for the Moon, since no Mars standard exists yet, so it is a reference only.

Data limits: Our terrain model has 20 m cells, so it cannot show boulders or small cliffs, and radiation dose at Jezero is not yet included. Slope is a stand-in for hazards and does not guarantee safety.

Time and distance: Long trips are shown as rover-assisted. A route "fits" in a spacewalk only if at least 2 hours remain on site for sampling.

Source quality: Every layer, place name and weather reading is linked to a USGS, IAU or NASA source.
dataRefs: Mars 2020 Science Investigation CTX DEM Mosaic (USGS Astrogeology and NASA Planetary Data System, from NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX images). Used for elevation, slope and relief shading of Jezero Crater.
NASA: First weather report from Jezero Crater (Perseverance MEDA weather station). Used for temperature, air pressure and wind conditions.
NASA: Everything is Dust in the Wind (Perseverance MEDA). Used for dust conditions at Jezero.
NASA NTRS: Exploration EVA Testing and Analogs (lunar surface suit requirements). Used as a reference for the 20° slope limit, spacewalk length and walking speed.
projectRefs: IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature (USGS Astrogeology): place names and coordinates for Jezero, Neretva Vallis, Sava Vallis and Pliva Vallis.
Universe Today: Mars surface gravity reference.
